common.schemalessNote: node-ldapjs has no schema subsystem and this directory is schemaless on purpose, so this is a VOCABULARY rather than a constraint: nothing rejects an entry for disobeying it.
apps.digestRdn: the identifier is too long for a readable RDN, so the cn is a digest of it and appIdentifier is the identity
apps.intro: {count} of a maximum {max} under {container}: every OAuth client, OpenID Connect relying party, SAML service provider, WS-Federation application, WS-Trust relying party, OpenID4VP verifier and Kerberos service this instance has been asked about. One entry per unique identifier, so an application that speaks two protocols under one name is one row with two kinds rather than two rows.
apps.registryNote: These entries are the registry, not a copy of one. An ldapmodify here changes what the protocol endpoints do: add a value to oauthRedirectUri and RFC 9700 mode accepts that redirect URI by exact match on the next authorization request. Nothing caches them. To EDIT one,
apps.registryNoteEnd: is the page with the controls on it; this one is the dump.
apps.placeholder: an identifier, a name, a DN or any value
apps.noMatch: No application matches. The filter above may be hiding some.
apps.nothingYet: Nothing yet. An entry appears the first time a client_id, wtrealm, AppliesTo, entityID or service principal name is accepted.
apps.schemaNote: node-ldapjs has no schema subsystem — it is protocol machinery, and it is a submodule this repository does not modify — and this directory is schemaless on purpose. So this is a VOCABULARY rather than a constraint: nothing rejects an entry for disobeying it. Where a registered class fits, it is used.
apps.attrNote: multi accumulates a repeat, single is assigned — which is what stops a counter growing a value per sign-in. Two attributes hold CREDENTIALS in the clear, for the reason /krb5/principals prints the Kerberos passwords; they are never written to the audit log.
apps.footControls: the same registry with the controls on it
fed.intro: {count} of a maximum {max} under {container}: the foreign identity providers this service consumes assertions from, and the foreign service providers it asserts to. One relationship is one DIRECTION, so a partner in both is two entries.
fed.warn: An ldapmodify here is a security change, which is not true of any other container in this directory. fedSigningCertificate decides whose assertions this service will believe; fedEnabled turns a partner on. Everywhere else here an edit changes what this service hands out, and every bind to this directory succeeds — so this container is exactly as protected as the rest of it, which is to say not at all. That is the honest state of a mock, and it is why federation is the one feature here that refuses by default.
fed.placeholder: an id, a DN, a protocol or a direction
fed.noMatch: No relationship matches. The filter above may be hiding some.
fed.nothingYet: Nothing yet, and nothing will appear by itself: unlike every other container here, this one is CONFIGURED. Add a relationship on
fed.attrNote: multi accumulates a repeat, single is assigned. The role column says which direction an attribute is for; one belonging to the other direction is refused by the console and by the management API, and an ldapmodify can still write it, where it will be ignored. fedClientSecret is THIS SERVICE'S OWN CREDENTIAL AT THE PARTNER — a real secret at a real foreign service, which is a stronger statement than anything else in this directory — and it is here in the clear for the reason /krb5/principals prints the Kerberos passwords. It is never written to the audit log and never shown in the console.
spiffe.intro: Registration entries live under {entries} and attested agents under {agents}.
spiffe.pagedNote: Both tables below are paged separately and they share this size. Changing it starts each of them at its first page.
spiffe.entryPlaceholder: spiffe://…, or part of a DN
spiffe.agentPlaceholder: an agent SPIFFE ID, or part of a DN
spiffe.attrNote: Declared is what an entry may DO and is editable from the console; derived is what HAPPENED and is not. ldapmodify reaches everything either way — refusing it in the console is the difference between offering an operation and merely not preventing it.
spiffe.footEntries: the entries as the console edits them
devices.intro: {count} under {container}: every device this realm knows, each owned by one person or one application. The same register
devices.note: These entries ARE the register: nothing caches them, so an ldapmodify here is what the next read sees. One value is withheld on this page as from every LDAP read: stsDeviceSecretHash, the verifier of a Native SSO device_secret. A key's JSON is public material and is shown whole.
devices.placeholder: an id, a DN, an owner or any value
devices.noMatch: No device matches. The filter above may be hiding some.
devices.noneYet: None yet. A Native SSO sign-in makes one, and an administrator can register one on
devices.attrNote: multi holds several values; single one. Several hold ONE JSON VALUE each: a key, the last compliance and status change, and the enrolment. common/devices.ts argues the layout.
roles.intro: {count} of a maximum {max} under {container}: one entry per role, and everything on it is MEMBERSHIP — who holds it. A person, a group and an application are all first-class members, which is what lets a client_credentials grant with no person in it be decided at all.
roles.note: Half the feature is not in this container. A role has two relations and they live apart on purpose: MEMBERSHIP is here, and the REQUIREMENT — which roles an application demands before anything is issued for it — is appRequiredRole on the application's own entry under ou=applications. So nothing in this container refuses anybody by itself, and a reader looking here for the reason somebody was turned away is one container across from it.
roles.noteMiddle: is the page with both halves and the controls on it;
roles.noteEnd: is where the other half is stored.
roles.placeholder: a role name, a DN, or a member
roles.noMatch: No role matches. The filter above may be hiding some.
roles.nothingYet: Nothing yet, which is the ORDINARY state rather than an empty one: an application that names no required role requires EVERYBODY, everybody holds EVERYBODY, and nothing is refused. A role is made on the Roles page or through POST /admin-api/roles/create-role.
roles.builtInHeading: The six that are in no container
roles.builtInNote: These are COMPUTED from the context of the decision being made rather than stored, so they have no entry here, no members to list, and cannot be created, edited or deleted. They are the reason an empty container above is not the feature being switched off: EVERYBODY is what an application requires when its entry names nothing, and everybody holds it.
roles.footControls: the same register with the controls on it
policies.intro: {count} of a maximum {max} under {container}: one entry per policy or policy set, holding the XACML document itself. Exactly one of them is the ROOT — a PDP evaluates one document and reaches the rest through PolicyIdReference.
policies.warn: A write here skips the typechecker, which is not true of any other door into this repository. Every write through
policies.warnEnd: and /admin-api/xacml parses the document and statically typechecks it, so a policy that does not typecheck is refused at WRITE time instead of going Indeterminate on every request. An ldapmodify of xacmlPolicyDocument reaches the entry directly and skips that, and nothing caches these entries — so the next request is decided against whatever was written.
policies.placeholder: a name, a DN, a PolicyId or anything in the document
policies.noMatch: No policy matches. The filter above may be hiding some.
policies.nothingYet: Nothing yet. A repository with no policies in it answers NotApplicable to every request, which a PEP turns into a refusal or an allow according to its bias.
policies.footControls: the same repository with the controls on it
peps.intro: {count} of a maximum {max} under {container}: the remote Policy Enforcement Points that have registered with this PDP. Each holds its own copy of the engine, pulls the policy repository, and decides in its own process.
peps.note: An empty container is not a feature that is off. A remote PEP pulls GET /xacml/pep/policies and converges whether or not it ever registers; registering is what buys it the change nudge and a row here. And an identity in this container was taken from the CLIENT CERTIFICATE the PEP presented, never from the body it sent — so a PEP cannot name itself anything it cannot prove.
peps.noteEnd: is the page with the controls on it.
peps.placeholder: a name, a DN, a certificate subject or a URL
peps.noMatch: No PEP matches. The filter above may be hiding some.
peps.nothingYet: Nothing has registered. Policy distribution is unaffected: a PEP that pulls GET /xacml/pep/policies without registering converges on the same repository and appears nowhere.
peps.footControls: the same registry with the controls on it
directory.intro: {count} entry/entries under {base}. This page is not LDAP — it is this service showing its own store, which is how you can tell an empty directory from a search filter that matched nothing.
directory.placeholder: a DN, an attribute name, or a value
directory.searchNote: The box matches the DN, any attribute NAME and any attribute VALUE, case-insensitively. Values are searched because the reader who needs this most often has a thumbprint or a secret in hand and no idea which entry carries it, which a search over DNs alone cannot answer.
directory.filterHiding: The filter above may be hiding some.
directory.clipNote: A value too long for its column is shortened, and the whole of it is one hover away. Hovering a shortened value opens a box holding it in full; one click inside that box selects all of it, so it can be copied. Nothing is lost by the shortening — ?format=json below is the whole store with nothing cut, and the full value is in this page’s markup either way.
service.persistLdif: an RFC 2849 LDIF file per realm in {dir}
service.transportValue: plain TCP on {port}, and LDAPS — TLS from the first byte — on {ldapsPort}. There is no StartTLS: it is an extended operation and this library implements none.
service.persistNone: NONE — this directory is in memory and goes when the process does, which is what this service did until 2026-08-27. Set persistence.mode to ldif (a file per realm, no database) or postgres (a shared store) to change that.
service.neverPersisted: Sessions, tokens, codes, artifacts and tickets are NEVER persisted in any mode.
service.listenerDown: DOWN — {why}. This page is HTTP and answers either way; the directory does not.
service.ldapsDown: DOWN — {why}. The two sockets are independent, so this says nothing about the one above.
service.intro: LDAPv3 over TCP {ldapPort}, and over TLS on {ldapsPort}, RFC 4511. A browser cannot speak it — the debugger’s api opens the socket. What the sockets are SET to is
service.introEnd: ; this page is what actually happened when this process tried to bind them.
service.ldapsHeading: LDAPS, and what it does not change
service.ldapsNote: Port {port} is the same directory over TLS — the same entries, the same handlers, the same every-bind-succeeds. What TLS adds is that the password is not on the wire in the clear; it does not make it checked. The certificate is the one the HTTPS listeners serve:
service.fetchItEnd: and put it in your truststore — LDAPTLS_REQCERT=never is the habit this endpoint exists to avoid, and it would also hide the one thing worth checking here.
service.noStartTls: There is no StartTLS: it is an extended operation (RFC 4511 §4.14) and ldapjs implements none, and this service does not patch that submodule. LDAPS is the one of the two no RFC defines — RFC 4513 standardised StartTLS and left ldaps:// as the de-facto scheme every client speaks anyway.
service.referentialNote: And one thing it does not: deleting a user leaves its DN in every group that lists it as a member. Referential integrity is a directory feature, not a protocol rule.
service.containersNote: The tree has three containers. ou=users holds people, one per identity that has authenticated here through any protocol. ou=groups holds groups, which grant nothing. ou=applications holds the OTHER side of those authentications — every OAuth client, relying party, service provider and Kerberos service this service has been asked about — and it is different from the other two in one way worth knowing: it is a registry rather than a record. The RFC 7591 client registrations live there and nothing caches them, so an ldapmodify of an application entry changes what the protocol endpoints do.
